"The reasoning was incorrect but it still arrived at the correct answer"

This is like how my math teacher would mark my answer wrong bc I did not show my work

The LLM does the work in it's head first

and then it shows it work, which is a different problem than finding the correct answer


To fix this we must either decide that all the work the model does in its head should be included as part of the solution finding process including what may seem like unnecessary and/or irrelevant spurious steps as it directly relates to that single question

or accept that when asked to show it's work that this is a different and seperate thing that should be evaluated apart from the solution output

Moreover, these models often BS their way towards solutions, with a "reasoning and justification" that I would not accept from even a weak undergrad. In some areas, these systems are very impressive, but there's still a long way to go.

comments.author: @PraiseNnadi-w3v
comments.text: I'll be more inclined to suspect actual reasoning once it solves problems it was never trained on. But then again, when an LLM tells you it's "reasoning", it is not telling you what it actually did. The "reasoning" itself is also just token prediction. That's why the answer may be correct but the "reasoning" was wrong. Because it's not actually saying how it got the answer but predicting what a reasonable explanation for the answer would be. This has been covered in Anthropic's On The Biology Of LLMs, Reasoning Models Don't Always Say What They Think, and Google's latest AI paper. People really need to understand this.

comments.text:
AI is a tool.

Just like a hammer hits harder than you — but doesn’t swing itself to drive nails.
Like a screwdriver, axe, drill, or forklift — each does its job better than your hands ever could.
The list goes on. These tools outperform us in physical tasks, and AI does the same for tasks involving text.

AI is still a tool. Even advanced AI systems — "Agents" — need someone (or another agent) to prompt them into action.

So, can AI replace most work that involves moving text around?
Yes. Just like machines replaced manual labor in moving dirt.

Can AI uncover things we didn’t think of?
Of course. It’s a powerful tool for discovery.

Will it want to destroy us all?
No. But like any tool, it can be used destructively — if prompted to.
You can stab someone with a screwdriver, but that’s not what it’s made for.

Our old tools augmented physical labor.
AI augments thought.
And if you have no thoughts of your own, it won’t be doing much augmenting.
